item.title: Crafting Shape in a Fluid World – The Intersection of Marketing and External Forces
item.content:encoded:
Marketing practice is being transformed by technological advances, geopolitical shifts, economic pressures, and growing demands for sustainability and social responsibility. Retail environments serve as key sites where these transformations unfold, with both physical and digital channels becoming laboratories for new consumer engagement and adaptive strategies. Consumers now demand greater brand ethics, transparency, and societal contributions, while external disruptions like supply chain fragility, inflation, and geopolitical tensions reshape pricing and sourcing. Simultaneously, artificial intelligence and platform ecosystems are fundamentally changing how consumers access information and make purchase decisions.

Appel publié par Journal of Consumer Marketing. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Consumer responses to global disruptions (e.g., inflation, supply chain fragility, climate events, tariffs, war)
  • Impact of AI, automation, and platform-based ecosystems on consumer well-being and happiness
  • How to enhance responsible consumption (e.g., reducing food waste and increasing adoptions of green energy and public transportation)
  • How to serve marginalized and disadvantaged consumers and enhance equality among gender, race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status through marketing and equitable practices
  • Evolving consumer purchase patterns and consumption practices around brand ethics, transparency, and sustainability
  • How firms can navigate sociopolitical activism (e.g., Should brands take a stand or remain silent?)
  • Recalibrating brand-consumer relationships in times of social and political polarization
  • Cross-cultural and cross-generational consumer insights in a post-globalization era
  • Retail innovation in response to external forces, trends, disruptions, and shifting consumer expectations
  • Marketing strategies for enhancing trust, loyalty, engagement in uncertain environments

Timeline

  • August 15, 2026: Opening date for manuscripts submissions
  • October 15, 2026: Closing date for manuscripts submission

item.title: The Future of the Global Space Industry: Business Strategy at the Intersection of Technology and Geopolitics
item.content:encoded:
Denis Leclerc, Thunderbird School of Global Management

Vanessa Farsadaki, Thunderbird School of Global Management

Daniel Thomas, Thunderbird School of Global Management

The global space industry is undergoing transformation driven by private companies and technological advances that have lowered costs and expanded space's strategic relevance. Advanced technologies including satellite miniaturization, artificial intelligence, and cloud computing now support diverse economic activities from telecommunications to climate monitoring. This evolution occurs within a complex geopolitical context where multiple nations are expanding their capabilities and international frameworks are being developed to govern competition in orbital environments.

This special issue seeks scholarly contributions examining the evolving global space economy and its implications for business strategy, international management, and governance. The journal particularly encourages submissions exploring cross-country dynamics, multinational enterprises, global value chains, and international frameworks shaping the commercial space sector, submitted as empirical research, theoretical work, comparative studies, policy analyses, or case studies.

Appel publié par Thunderbird International Business Review. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Artificial Intelligence and Digital Technologies in Space: The role of artificial intelligence in mission planning, autonomous navigation, and satellite operations; big data analytics and the commercialization of satellite data; the impact of AI and cloud infrastructure on the global space innovation ecosystem
  • Bioeconomics and Human Health: Biomedical research and pharmaceutical development in microgravity environments; advances in telemedicine and remote healthcare technologies derived from space research; implications of long-duration human spaceflight for global healthcare innovation
  • Public–Private Partnerships and Innovation Ecosystems: Collaboration between governments and private firms in space development; comparative analyses of national space strategies and partnership models; governance mechanisms that enable innovation while managing technological and financial risks
  • Geoeconomics and Global Collaboration: The role of space technologies in global development, climate monitoring, agriculture, and disaster response; the impact of geopolitical competition on international space collaboration; space as a domain of economic diplomacy and strategic competition
  • Strategy and Global Business Implications: Space-based technologies and new business models across industries; implications for global supply chains, telecommunications, and financial services; corporate strategy and international competition in emerging space markets

Timeline

  • September 15, 2026: Extended Abstract Submission Deadline
  • January 31, 2027: Full Manuscript Submission Deadline

item.title: Tourism and the 2026 Middle East Crisis: International and Regional Implications
item.content:encoded:
C. Michael Hall, Massey University

The ongoing Middle East conflict involving Israel, Iran, the United States, Lebanon, and Palestine represents the most significant disruption to international tourism since COVID-19. Its effects extend globally through disrupted aviation hubs in the Gulf, restricted airspace affecting Asia-Europe travel, and threats to shipping routes, alongside direct threats to tourism infrastructure worldwide.

Beyond direct military impacts, the crisis influences global tourism through elevated oil and energy costs, affecting aviation fuel prices and transport expenses. This energy crisis, reportedly exceeding previous major oil shocks combined, threatens airline viability and has implications for the sustainability and future trajectory of tourism infrastructure and carbon-dependent transport networks.

The journal invites research examining how the crisis affects tourist behavior, destination competitiveness, industry resilience, and government and business responses across international, regional, national, and local contexts, as well as its broader implications for tourism governance and energy futures.

Appel publié par Current Issues in Tourism. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • The effects of the Middle East crisis on international and domestic tourist attitudes, behaviour, decision-making, and flows
  • The impacts of the Middle East crisis on destinations, attractions and businesses and policy and industry responses
  • The Middle East crisis and destination image
  • Resilience, adaptation, and vulnerability in tourism considering the Middle East crisis
  • The geopolitics of tourism and the Middle East crisis
  • The Middle East crisis and the aviation sector
  • Energy futures for tourism
  • Foreign policy and tourism
  • The future of tourism in the Middle East and the Eastern Mediterranean
  • Substitute behaviour because of the Middle East crisis and the cost of energy

item.title: Digital Innovation, Geopolitics, and International Business
item.content:encoded:
Digital technologies are increasingly shaping the conduct of individuals, businesses, and societies. Particularly disruptive digital technologies include artificial intelligence, the internet of things, additive manufacturing, robotics, business analytics, cloud-based computing, and blockchain. Although digital technologies may appear geographically unanchored, they are physically situated in specific locations and connected through infrastructure such as underwater cables. The spatial embeddedness of these infrastructures has become intertwined with geopolitical competition and strategic rivalry, with control over critical assets such as undersea cables, semiconductor production hubs, cloud service locations, and digital standards increasingly contested between leading powers, notably the US and China.
